title: Trace the authorization code and refresh-token defenses
description: Switch scenarios to see which value crosses the browser, what remains secret, and where exact redirects, PKCE, or rotation stop replay.

nodes.label: User agent
nodes.detail: Carries the authorization request and one-time response. It should not receive a client secret, refresh token, or access token in a URL.

nodes.label: OAuth client
nodes.detail: Creates state and the PKCE verifier, stores them against the browser session, and validates the response before exchanging the code.

nodes.label: Authorization endpoint
nodes.detail: Authenticates as needed, obtains authorization, binds the code to client and redirect URI, and accepts only registered redirects.

nodes.label: Token endpoint
nodes.detail: Redeems a code once after validating client binding, redirect URI, and PKCE verifier; it also detects rotated refresh-token reuse.

nodes.label: Resource server
nodes.detail: Accepts tokens only from the expected issuer and for its audience, then enforces scope and resource-level authorization.

nodes.label: Token/session store
nodes.detail: Keeps verifier, one-time state, tokens, grant family, and application session data in the boundary appropriate to the client type.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.detail: May steal a code, tamper with a redirect, or replay an invalidated refresh token. Each scenario shows the server-side rejection point.

scenarios.label: Happy code flow
scenarios.summary: The client starts one transaction, the authorization server returns a one-time code, and the client redeems it with the matching PKCE verifier.
scenarios.result: The access token is issued only at the token endpoint. The browser carries the code, while the transaction-specific verifier remains under the client's control.

scenarios.label: Stolen code
scenarios.summary: An attacker obtains the authorization code but does not have the transaction's high-entropy verifier.
scenarios.result: The token endpoint rejects the exchange because the attacker's verifier does not produce the challenge bound to the code. A client secret embedded in a public app would not provide this protection.

scenarios.label: Redirect mismatch
scenarios.summary: An attacker changes the requested callback to an unregistered URI in an attempt to receive the authorization response.
scenarios.result: Exact string matching rejects the request before a code is sent. Native loopback redirects have the standards-defined dynamic-port exception; broad wildcard callbacks do not.

scenarios.label: Refresh reuse
scenarios.summary: After rotation, the legitimate client uses the current refresh token while an attacker replays an invalidated token from the same grant family.
scenarios.result: Reuse reveals that the refresh-token family is compromised. The authorization server revokes the active family, stopping the attacker and forcing the legitimate client through a new authorization grant.
